claim: Adaptive immunity vitally depends on major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC I) molecules loaded with peptides.
source: Adaptive immunity vitally depends on major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC I) molecules loaded with peptides.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the immune system.

claim: Selective loading of peptides onto MHC I, referred to as peptide editing, is catalyzed by tapasin and the tapasin-related TAPBPR.
source: Selective loading of peptides onto MHC I, referred to as peptide editing, is catalyzed by tapasin and the tapasin-related TAPBPR.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: An important catalytic role has been ascribed to a structural feature in TAPBPR called the scoop loop.
source: An important catalytic role has been ascribed to a structural feature in TAPBPR called the scoop loop, but the exact function of the scoop loop remains elusive.
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: The scoop loop of TAPBPR contributes substantially to the stability of the MHC I-chaperone complex.
source: Here, using a reconstituted system of defined peptide-exchange components including human TAPBPR variants, we uncover a substantial contribution of the scoop loop to the stability of the MHC I-chaperone complex and to peptide editing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically SEC analyses showing reduced complex stability for scoop loop variants.

claim: The scoop loop of TAPBPR contributes substantially to peptide editing.
source: Here, using a reconstituted system of defined peptide-exchange components including human TAPBPR variants, we uncover a substantial contribution of the scoop loop to the stability of the MHC I-chaperone complex and to peptide editing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from peptide exchange assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: The scoop loop of TAPBPR functions as an internal peptide surrogate in peptide-depleted environments stabilizing empty MHC I.
source: We reveal that the scoop loop of TAPBPR functions as an internal peptide surrogate in peptide-depleted environments stabilizing empty MHC I and impeding peptide rebinding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-step peptide exchange assays and SEC analyses.

claim: The scoop loop of TAPBPR impedes peptide rebinding.
source: We reveal that the scoop loop of TAPBPR functions as an internal peptide surrogate in peptide-depleted environments stabilizing empty MHC I and impeding peptide rebinding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-step peptide exchange assays showing differential peptide release.

claim: The scoop loop acts as an additional selectivity filter in shaping the repertoire of presented peptide epitopes.
source: The scoop loop thereby acts as an additional selectivity filter in shaping the repertoire of presented peptide epitopes and the formation of a hierarchical immune response.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing differential peptide release and rebinding.

claim: Nucleated cells of higher vertebrates present a selection of endogenous peptides on MHC I molecules at the cell surface.
source: Nucleated cells of higher vertebrates provide information about their health status by presenting a selection of endogenous peptides on MHC I molecules at the cell surface.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about MHC I antigen presentation.

claim: CD8+ T lymphocytes are able to detect and eliminate infected or cancerous cells by sampling peptide-MHC I complexes.
source: By sampling these peptide-MHC I (pMHC I) complexes, CD8+ T lymphocytes are able to detect and eliminate infected or cancerous cells (Blum et al., 2013; Rock et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Peptide editing is catalyzed by the two homologous MHC I-specific chaperones tapasin (Tsn) and TAP-binding protein-related (TAPBPR).
source: In a process called peptide editing or proofreading, peptides derived from the cellular proteome are selected for their ability to form stable pMHC I complexes. This peptide editing is known to be catalyzed by the two homologous MHC I-specific chaperones tapasin (Tsn) and TAP-binding protein-related (TAPBPR) (Fleischmann et al., 2015; Hermann et al., 2015; Morozov et al., 2016; Neerincx and Boyle, 2017; Tan et al., 2002; Thomas and Tampé, 2019; Wearsch and Cresswell, 2007; Wearsch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The selection of high-affinity MHC I-associated peptide epitopes is of pivotal importance for immunosurveillance by effector T lymphocytes.
source: The selection of high-affinity MHC I-associated peptide epitopes is of pivotal importance not only for immunosurveillance by effector T lymphocytes, but also for priming of naïve T cells and T cell differentiation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about adaptive immunity.

claim: The selection of high-affinity MHC I-associated peptide epitopes is of pivotal importance for priming of naïve T cells and T cell differentiation.
source: The selection of high-affinity MHC I-associated peptide epitopes is of pivotal importance not only for immunosurveillance by effector T lymphocytes, but also for priming of naïve T cells and T cell differentiation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about adaptive immunity.

claim: Tapasin functions as an integral constituent of the peptide-loading complex (PLC) in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane.
source: As an integral constituent of the peptide-loading complex (PLC) in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane, the ER-restricted Tsn functions in a 'nanocompartment' characterized by a high concentration of diverse, optimal peptides.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the PLC.

claim: Tapasin is ER-restricted.
source: As an integral constituent of the peptide-loading complex (PLC) in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane, the ER-restricted Tsn functions in a 'nanocompartment' characterized by a high concentration of diverse, optimal peptides.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about tapasin localization.

claim: Tapasin functions in a 'nanocompartment' characterized by a high concentration of diverse, optimal peptides.
source: As an integral constituent of the peptide-loading complex (PLC) in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane, the ER-restricted Tsn functions in a 'nanocompartment' characterized by a high concentration of diverse, optimal peptides.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the PLC environment.

claim: Peptides are shuttled into the ER by the heterodimeric ABC transporter associated with antigen processing TAP1/2.
source: The peptides are shuttled into the ER by the heterodimeric ABC (ATP-binding cassette) transporter associated with antigen processing TAP1/2, the central component of the PLC (Abele and Tampé, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: TAP1/2 is the central component of the PLC.
source: The peptides are shuttled into the ER by the heterodimeric ABC (ATP-binding cassette) transporter associated with antigen processing TAP1/2, the central component of the PLC (Abele and Tampé, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In the ER, most peptides are further trimmed by the aminopeptidases ERAP1 and ERAP2 to an optimal length for binding in the MHC I groove.
source: In the ER, most peptides are further trimmed by the aminopeptidases ERAP1 and ERAP2 to an optimal length for binding in the MHC I groove (Evnouchidou and van Endert, 2019; Hammer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TAPBPR operates independently of the PLC.
source: In contrast to Tsn, TAPBPR operates independently of the PLC and is also found in the peptide-depleted cis-Golgi network (Boyle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: TAPBPR is found in the peptide-depleted cis-Golgi network.
source: In contrast to Tsn, TAPBPR operates independently of the PLC and is also found in the peptide-depleted cis-Golgi network (Boyle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A recent cryo-EM study of the fully-assembled human PLC provided fundamental insights into the architecture and dynamic nature of the Tsn-containing PLC.
source: Fundamental insights into the architecture and dynamic nature of the Tsn-containing PLC have come from a recent cryo-EM study of the fully-assembled human PLC (Blees et al., 2017), while the basic principles underlying catalyzed peptide editing have been elucidated by crystal structures of the TAPBPR-MHC I complex (Jiang et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2017a):
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Crystal structures of the TAPBPR-MHC I complex elucidated the basic principles underlying catalyzed peptide editing.
source: Fundamental insights into the architecture and dynamic nature of the Tsn-containing PLC have come from a recent cryo-EM study of the fully-assembled human PLC (Blees et al., 2017), while the basic principles underlying catalyzed peptide editing have been elucidated by crystal structures of the TAPBPR-MHC I complex (Jiang et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2017a):
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TAPBPR stabilizes the peptide-binding groove in a widened conformation primarily through the MHC I α2–1 helix.
source: TAPBPR stabilizes the peptide-binding groove in a widened conformation primarily through the MHC I α2–1 helix, distorts the floor of the binding groove, and shifts the position of β2-microglobulin (β2m).
evidence: This is based on crystal structures cited in the manuscript.

claim: TAPBPR distorts the floor of the MHC I binding groove.
source: TAPBPR stabilizes the peptide-binding groove in a widened conformation primarily through the MHC I α2–1 helix, distorts the floor of the binding groove, and shifts the position of β2-microglobulin (β2m).
evidence: This is based on crystal structures cited in the manuscript.

claim: TAPBPR shifts the position of β2-microglobulin (β2m).
source: TAPBPR stabilizes the peptide-binding groove in a widened conformation primarily through the MHC I α2–1 helix, distorts the floor of the binding groove, and shifts the position of β2-microglobulin (β2m).
evidence: This is based on crystal structures cited in the manuscript.

claim: One of the two TAPBPR-MHC I complex structures revealed a structural feature in TAPBPR named the scoop loop.
source: Furthermore, one of the two TAPBPR-MHC I complex structures revealed a remarkable structural feature in TAPBPR named the scoop loop (Thomas and Tampé, 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The scoop loop in TAPBPR is significantly longer than the corresponding region in Tsn.
source: In TAPBPR, this loop is significantly longer than the corresponding region in Tsn, which was not resolved in the X-ray structure of Tsn (Dong et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on comparison of crystal structures cited in the manuscript.

claim: The corresponding region to the scoop loop in Tsn was not resolved in the X-ray structure of Tsn.
source: In TAPBPR, this loop is significantly longer than the corresponding region in Tsn, which was not resolved in the X-ray structure of Tsn (Dong et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The scoop loop of TAPBPR is located in the F-pocket region of the empty MHC I binding groove.
source: Notably, the scoop loop of TAPBPR is located in the F-pocket region of the empty MHC I binding groove (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and Figure 1A,B.

claim: The F pocket region is crucially involved in defining pMHC I stability by anchoring the C-terminal part of the peptide.
source: By anchoring the C-terminal part of the peptide, the F pocket region is crucially involved in defining pMHC I stability (Abualrous et al., 2015; Hein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The scoop loop occupies a position that is incompatible with peptide binding.
source: The scoop loop occupies a position that is incompatible with peptide binding and displaces or coordinates several key MHC I residues responsible for binding the C terminus of the peptide.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure cited in the manuscript.

claim: The scoop loop displaces or coordinates several key MHC I residues responsible for binding the C terminus of the peptide.
source: The scoop loop occupies a position that is incompatible with peptide binding and displaces or coordinates several key MHC I residues responsible for binding the C terminus of the peptide.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure cited in the manuscript.

claim: The scoop loop can be regarded as a surrogate for the C terminus of the displaced peptide, stabilizing the inherently labile empty MHC I molecule.
source: We therefore proposed that the scoop loop can be regarded as a surrogate for the C terminus of the displaced peptide, stabilizing the inherently labile empty MHC I molecule (Thomas and Tampé, 2017a).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: By occupying a region critical to peptide binding, the scoop loop might allow only high-affinity peptides to re-enter the MHC I binding groove after displacement of sub-optimal peptide.
source: At the same time, by occupying a region critical to peptide binding, the scoop loop might allow only high-affinity peptides to re-enter the MHC I binding groove after displacement of sub-optimal peptide.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on structural observations.

claim: Ilca et al. investigated TAPBPR scoop-loop variants using immunopeptidomics and cell-based assays.
source: The proposed importance of the scoop loop for TAPBPR function has recently been scrutinized in a study by Ilca et al. investigating TAPBPR scoop-loop variants using immunopeptidomics and cell-based assays (Ilca et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Ilca et al. found that a specific leucine residue in the scoop loop facilitates peptide displacement on MHC I allomorphs favoring hydrophobic peptide side chains in their F pocket.
source: Ilca et al. found that a specific leucine residue in the scoop loop facilitates peptide displacement on MHC I allomorphs favoring hydrophobic peptide side chains in their F pocket.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The scoop loop is of critical importance for TAPBPR-mediated stabilization of empty MHC I clients in peptide-depleted environments.
source: We demonstrate that the scoop loop is of critical importance for TAPBPR-mediated stabilization of empty MHC I clients in peptide-depleted environments and contributes to peptide quality control during editing by impeding released peptide to rebind in the MHC I groove.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from SEC analyses and peptide exchange assays.

claim: The scoop loop contributes to peptide quality control during editing by impeding released peptide to rebind in the MHC I groove.
source: We demonstrate that the scoop loop is of critical importance for TAPBPR-mediated stabilization of empty MHC I clients in peptide-depleted environments and contributes to peptide quality control during editing by impeding released peptide to rebind in the MHC I groove.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-step peptide exchange assays.

claim: The TAPBPR scoop loop has a crucial role in establishing a hierarchical immune response.
source: Collectively, our data support a crucial role for the TAPBPR scoop loop in establishing a hierarchical immune response.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing the scoop loop's role in peptide selection.

claim: TAPBPRTsn-SL and TAPBPRΔSL are competent to form complexes with MHC I.
source: Subsequent SEC analysis revealed that both TAPBPRTsn-SL and TAPBPRΔSL are, in principle, competent to form complexes with MHC I (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: After reanalysis of the MHC I chaperone complexes by SEC, the mutant complexes were mostly dissociated, indicating kinetic instability.
source: After reanalysis of the MHC I chaperone complexes by SEC, the mutant complexes were mostly dissociated, indicating kinetic instability (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Isolation and reinjection of the wt complex showed that it remained stable for the duration of the experiment.
source: In contrast, isolation and reinjection of the wt complex showed that it remained stable for the duration of the experiment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: In the presence of a high-affinity peptide, the TAPBPRwt-MHC I complex dissociated.
source: Yet, in the presence of a high-affinity peptide, even the TAPBPRwt-MHC I complex dissociated, in accordance with the role of TAPBPR as a chaperone that stabilizes the MHC I as long as no optimal peptide is present (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The scoop loop is crucial to an extended lifetime of the chaperone-client complex, enabling the escorting of empty MHC I by TAPBPR in a peptide-deficient environment.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that the scoop loop is crucial to an extended lifetime of the chaperone-client complex, enabling the escorting of empty MHC I by TAPBPR in a peptide-deficient environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced complex stability for scoop loop variants.

claim: TAPBPRwt and the scoop-loop variants accelerated the uncatalyzed peptide release from H2-Db to a similar extent.
source: For the mouse MHC I allomorph H2-Db, TAPBPRwt and the scoop-loop variants accelerated the uncatalyzed peptide release (2.53 ± 0.37 × 10−3 s−1) to a similar extent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from peptide exchange assays.

claim: The TAPBPRΔSL mutant lacking the entire scoop loop exhibited slightly reduced activity (7.68 ± 1.17 × 10−3 s−1) compared to the wt protein (10.41 ± 0.54 × 10−3 s−1) in peptide displacement from H2-Db.
source: The TAPBPRΔSL mutant lacking the entire scoop loop exhibited slightly reduced activity (7.68 ± 1.17 × 10−3 s−1) compared to the wt protein (10.41 ± 0.54 × 10−3 s−1), whereas TAPBPRTsn-SL was slightly more active (12.64 ± 1.03 × 10−3 s−1) (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: TAPBPRTsn-SL was slightly more active (12.64 ± 1.03 × 10−3 s−1) than TAPBPRwt in peptide displacement from H2-Db.
source: The TAPBPRΔSL mutant lacking the entire scoop loop exhibited slightly reduced activity (7.68 ± 1.17 × 10−3 s−1) compared to the wt protein (10.41 ± 0.54 × 10−3 s−1), whereas TAPBPRTsn-SL was slightly more active (12.64 ± 1.03 × 10−3 s−1) (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: When the experiment was performed at a much lower TAPBPR concentration (75 nM), the TAPBPRs retained their activity, and the gradual activity differences between the variants remained.
source: When we performed the experiment at a much lower TAPBPR concentration (75 nM), the TAPBPRs retained their activity, and the gradual activity differences between the variants remained (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAPBPRwt and the scoop-loop mutants have similar affinities for H2-Db.
source: This suggests that TAPBPRwt and the scoop-loop mutants have similar affinities for H2-Db.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing retained activity at low TAPBPR concentrations.

claim: TAPBPRwt was able to catalyze displacement of a high-affinity peptide from H2-Db, although the catalytic effect was considerably smaller (1.8-fold acceleration) than for H2-Db loaded with the medium-affinity peptide (4.1-fold acceleration).
source: TAPBPRwt was even able to catalyze displacement of a high-affinity peptide from H2-Db, although the catalytic effect was considerably smaller (1.8-fold acceleration) than for H2-Db loaded with the medium-affinity peptide (4.1-fold acceleration) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: In a peptide-rich environment (1000-fold molar excess of peptide), the highest catalytic activity towards HLA-A*02:01 was observed for TAPBPRTsn-SL, followed by TAPBPRwt and TAPBPRΔSL.
source: Similar to the experiments with H2-Db, in a peptide-rich environment (1000-fold molar excess of peptide), the highest catalytic activity towards HLA-A*02:01 was observed for TAPBPRTsn-SL, followed by TAPBPRwt and TAPBPRΔSL; yet, the differences in activity between the three TAPBPRs were more pronounced, and the acceleration of the uncatalyzed peptide dissociation from HLA-A*02:01 (1.90 ± 0.04 × 10−3 s−1) by TAPBPRTsn-SL (26.31 ± 2.59 × 10−3 s−1) and TAPBPRwt (15.79 ± 0.71 × 10−3 s−1) was significantly higher than for H2-Db, while the activity of TAPBPRΔSL (8.52 ± 1.18 × 10−3 s−1) remained almost the same (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: The differences in activity between the three TAPBPRs were more pronounced for HLA-A*02:01 than for H2-Db.
source: Similar to the experiments with H2-Db, in a peptide-rich environment (1000-fold molar excess of peptide), the highest catalytic activity towards HLA-A*02:01 was observed for TAPBPRTsn-SL, followed by TAPBPRwt and TAPBPRΔSL; yet, the differences in activity between the three TAPBPRs were more pronounced, and the acceleration of the uncatalyzed peptide dissociation from HLA-A*02:01 (1.90 ± 0.04 × 10−3 s−1) by TAPBPRTsn-SL (26.31 ± 2.59 × 10−3 s−1) and TAPBPRwt (15.79 ± 0.71 × 10−3 s−1) was significantly higher than for H2-Db, while the activity of TAPBPRΔSL (8.52 ± 1.18 × 10−3 s−1) remained almost the same (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: The acceleration of the uncatalyzed peptide dissociation from HLA-A*02:01 by TAPBPRTsn-SL and TAPBPRwt was significantly higher than for H2-Db.
source: Similar to the experiments with H2-Db, in a peptide-rich environment (1000-fold molar excess of peptide), the highest catalytic activity towards HLA-A*02:01 was observed for TAPBPRTsn-SL, followed by TAPBPRwt and TAPBPRΔSL; yet, the differences in activity between the three TAPBPRs were more pronounced, and the acceleration of the uncatalyzed peptide dissociation from HLA-A*02:01 (1.90 ± 0.04 × 10−3 s−1) by TAPBPRTsn-SL (26.31 ± 2.59 × 10−3 s−1) and TAPBPRwt (15.79 ± 0.71 × 10−3 s−1) was significantly higher than for H2-Db, while the activity of TAPBPRΔSL (8.52 ± 1.18 × 10−3 s−1) remained almost the same (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: The activity of TAPBPRΔSL towards HLA-A*02:01 (8.52 ± 1.18 × 10−3 s−1) remained almost the same as for H2-Db.
source: Similar to the experiments with H2-Db, in a peptide-rich environment (1000-fold molar excess of peptide), the highest catalytic activity towards HLA-A*02:01 was observed for TAPBPRTsn-SL, followed by TAPBPRwt and TAPBPRΔSL; yet, the differences in activity between the three TAPBPRs were more pronounced, and the acceleration of the uncatalyzed peptide dissociation from HLA-A*02:01 (1.90 ± 0.04 × 10−3 s−1) by TAPBPRTsn-SL (26.31 ± 2.59 × 10−3 s−1) and TAPBPRwt (15.79 ± 0.71 × 10−3 s−1) was significantly higher than for H2-Db, while the activity of TAPBPRΔSL (8.52 ± 1.18 × 10−3 s−1) remained almost the same (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: TN3-Ala and TN6 displayed drastically reduced activity towards H2-Db in the peptide-exchange experiment, with peptide dissociation rate constants close to the value of the uncatalyzed reaction.
source: Consequently, TN3-Ala and TN6 displayed drastically reduced activity towards H2-Db in our peptide-exchange experiment, with peptide dissociation rate constants close to the value of the uncatalyzed reaction (Figure 3C,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3C and 3F.

claim: Under peptide-rich condition, the tested TAPBPR variants differ gradually in their displacement activity in an allomorph-dependent manner.
source: In summary, the results of our exchange assays demonstrate that under peptide-rich condition, the tested TAPBPR variants differ gradually in their displacement activity in an allomorph-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from peptide exchange assays with H2-Db and HLA-A*02:01.

claim: The TAPBPRΔSL mutant lacking the scoop loop is still able to substantially accelerate peptide dissociation from MHC I.
source: But even the TAPBPRΔSL mutant lacking the scoop loop is still able to substantially accelerate peptide dissociation from MHC I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from peptide exchange assays.

claim: In the TAPBPR-MHC I crystal structure, the scoop loop binds in the F pocket region of the MHC binding groove and appears to act as a surrogate for the peptide C terminus.
source: In the TAPBPR-MHC I crystal structure, the scoop loop binds in the F pocket region of the MHC binding groove and appears to act as a surrogate for the peptide C terminus (Thomas and Tampé, 2017a).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure cited in the manuscript.

claim: After addition of the different TAPBPRs to H2-Db loaded with fluorescent peptide, the polarization changes diverged dramatically.
source: Strikingly, after addition of the different TAPBPRs to H2-Db loaded with fluorescent peptide, the polarization changes, which correspond to the changes in the ratio of free to bound peptide, diverged dramatically (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Peptide dissociation was most pronounced for TAPBPRwt with the native scoop loop, reaching ~ 60% peptide release from H2-Db.
source: Peptide dissociation was most pronounced for TAPBPRwt with the native scoop loop, reaching ~ 60% peptide release, whereas only ~ 12% of the peptide population was released from H2-Db by TAPBPRTsn-SL, and almost no decrease in polarization was caused by TAPBPRΔSL.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-step peptide exchange assays.

claim: Only ~ 12% of the peptide population was released from H2-Db by TAPBPRTsn-SL.
source: Peptide dissociation was most pronounced for TAPBPRwt with the native scoop loop, reaching ~ 60% peptide release, whereas only ~ 12% of the peptide population was released from H2-Db by TAPBPRTsn-SL, and almost no decrease in polarization was caused by TAPBPRΔSL.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-step peptide exchange assays.

claim: Almost no decrease in polarization was caused by TAPBPRΔSL in the two-step peptide exchange assay with H2-Db.
source: Peptide dissociation was most pronounced for TAPBPRwt with the native scoop loop, reaching ~ 60% peptide release, whereas only ~ 12% of the peptide population was released from H2-Db by TAPBPRTsn-SL, and almost no decrease in polarization was caused by TAPBPRΔSL.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-step peptide exchange assays.

claim: TAPBPRTsn-SL-induced peptide dissociation from HLA-A*02:01 was significantly stronger than from H2-Db, approaching the level of peptide release induced by TAPBPRwt.
source: Similar to our original peptide exchange assay (Figure 3), differences between the two MHC I allomorphs were observed: In comparison to H2-Db, TAPBPRTsn-SL-induced peptide dissociation from HLA-A*02:01 was significantly stronger, approaching the level of peptide release induced by TAPBPRwt (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Peptide release was peptide-dependent, as H2-Db loaded with a high-affinity peptide led to a significantly smaller decline in bound peptide.
source: Peptide release was also peptide-dependent, as H2-Db loaded with a high-affinity peptide led to a significantly smaller decline in bound peptide (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: After addition of competitor peptide (2nd step), the observed dissociation rate constants were in the same range as the values determined for the one-step experiment.
source: After addition of competitor peptide (2nd step), the observed dissociation rate constants were in the same range as the values determined for the one-step experiment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from peptide exchange assays.

claim: The level of released peptide after TAPBPR addition was titratable and reached saturation at 3 µM TAPBPR.
source: Moreover, the level of released peptide after TAPBPR addition was titratable and reached saturation at 3 µM TAPBPR (Figure 4C–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C–E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Under the given conditions, TAPBPRwt was able to dissociate 70% of total H2-Db-associated peptide.
source: Under the given conditions, TAPBPRwt was able to dissociate 70% (H2-Db) and 80% (HLA-A*02:01) of total MHC I-associated peptide, respectively (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Under the given conditions, TAPBPRwt was able to dissociate 80% of total HLA-A*02:01-associated peptide.
source: Under the given conditions, TAPBPRwt was able to dissociate 70% (H2-Db) and 80% (HLA-A*02:01) of total MHC I-associated peptide, respectively (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The scoop loop interferes with re-binding of displaced peptide.
source: These results suggest that the scoop loop interferes with re-binding of displaced peptide.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing differential peptide release in the two-step assay.

claim: The scoop loop can only be completely dislodged from the MHC I binding pocket by a high-affinity peptide.
source: It can only be completely dislodged from the MHC I binding pocket by a high-affinity peptide.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that high-affinity peptides can displace TAPBPR.

claim: The scoop loop acts as a crucial selectivity filter during peptide editing on MHC I.
source: The scoop loop thus acts as a crucial selectivity filter during peptide editing on MHC I.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing the scoop loop's role in impeding peptide rebinding.

claim: The TAPBPR scoop loop is critically important in chaperoning intrinsically unstable empty MHC I clients in a peptide-depleted environment.
source: Here, we show that the TAPBPR scoop loop is indeed critically important in chaperoning intrinsically unstable empty MHC I clients in a peptide-depleted environment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from SEC analyses showing reduced complex stability for scoop loop variants.

claim: The reduced chaperone activity of TAPBPRTsn-SL is illustrated by the dramatically reduced lifetime of the TAPBPRΔSL complex.
source: This is illustrated by the reduced chaperone activity of TAPBPRTsn-SL, which harbors the shorter Tsn scoop loop, and by the dramatically reduced lifetime of the TAPBPRΔSL complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from SEC analyses.

claim: In a peptide-rich, PLC-like environment, the TAPBPRTsn-SL mutant displays the highest activity.
source: In a peptide-rich, PLC-like environment, emulated by our one-step displacement experiments, the TAPBPRTsn-SL mutant displays the highest activity, while TAPBPRΔSL retains the ability to displace peptide.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from one-step peptide exchange assays.

claim: TAPBPRΔSL retains the ability to displace peptide in a peptide-rich environment.
source: In a peptide-rich, PLC-like environment, emulated by our one-step displacement experiments, the TAPBPRTsn-SL mutant displays the highest activity, while TAPBPRΔSL retains the ability to displace peptide.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from one-step peptide exchange assays.

claim: The observation that TAPBPRΔSL retains the ability to displace peptide appears to be in contrast to the study by Ilca et al. which found that TAPBPR with a mutated, but full-length scoop loop loses its ability to effectively mediate peptide dissociation.
source: The latter observation appears to be in contrast to the study by Ilca et al. which found that TAPBPR with a mutated, but full-length scoop loop loses its ability to effectively mediate peptide dissociation (Ilca et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's findings and prior research.

claim: The TAPBPR scoop loop acts as an internal peptide competitor.
source: In addition to stabilizing the chaperone-MHC I complex, we demonstrate that the TAPBPR scoop loop acts as an internal peptide competitor, and thus, as a selectivity filter in the discrimination between low- and high-affinity peptides.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-step peptide exchange assays.

claim: The TAPBPR scoop loop acts as a selectivity filter in the discrimination between low- and high-affinity peptides.
source: In addition to stabilizing the chaperone-MHC I complex, we demonstrate that the TAPBPR scoop loop acts as an internal peptide competitor, and thus, as a selectivity filter in the discrimination between low- and high-affinity peptides.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-step peptide exchange assays.

claim: The peptide-filtering activity of the scoop loop seems to be allomorph-dependent for TAPBPRTsn-SL.
source: The peptide-filtering activity seems to be allomorph-dependent for TAPBPRTsn-SL.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing different peptide release levels for H2-Db and HLA-A*02:01.

claim: The Tsn scoop loop interacts more strongly with the F-pocket region of HLA-A*02:01 and is therefore able to impede peptide rebinding more efficiently than in the case of H2-Db.
source: Our current interpretation of this allomorph specificity is that the Tsn scoop loop interacts more strongly with the F-pocket region of HLA-A*02:01 and is therefore able to impede peptide rebinding more efficiently than in the case of H2-Db.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: TAPBPRwt shows a strong peptide release activity towards both H2-Db and HLA-A*02:01.
source: In contrast, TAPBPRwt shows a strong peptide release activity towards both MHC I allomorphs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-step peptide exchange assays.

claim: The large concave surface formed by the N-terminal domain of TAPBPR mediates its initial encounter with a suboptimally-loaded MHC I, assisted by the C-terminal domain of TAPBPR.
source: The large concave surface formed by the N-terminal domain of TAPBPR mediates its initial encounter with a suboptimally-loaded MHC I, assisted by the C-terminal domain of TAPBPR, which contacts the α3 domain of the MHC I heavy chain and β2m.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge from crystal structures.

claim: The C-terminal domain of TAPBPR contacts the α3 domain of the MHC I heavy chain and β2m.
source: The large concave surface formed by the N-terminal domain of TAPBPR mediates its initial encounter with a suboptimally-loaded MHC I, assisted by the C-terminal domain of TAPBPR, which contacts the α3 domain of the MHC I heavy chain and β2m.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge from crystal structures.

claim: TAPBPR facilitates the release of low- to medium-affinity peptides primarily by widening the peptide-binding groove through the MHC I α2–1-helix, fastening the peptide-coordinating Tyr84, distorting the floor of the binding groove, and shifting the position of β2m.
source: TAPBPR facilitates the release of low- to medium-affinity peptides primarily by widening the peptide-binding groove through the MHC I α2–1-helix, fastening the peptide-coordinating Tyr84, distorting the floor of the binding groove, and shifting the position of β2m (Jiang et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2017a).
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge from crystal structures cited in the manuscript.

claim: The remodeling of MHC I by TAPBPR is made possible by the intrinsic plasticity of MHC I molecules.
source: This remodeling is made possible by the intrinsic plasticity of MHC I molecules (Bailey et al., 2015; Garstka et al., 2011; McShan et al., 2019; Natarajan et al., 2018; Thomas and Tampé, 2017b; van Hateren et al., 2017; van Hateren et al., 2015; Wieczorek et al., 2017), and it appears to be induced primarily by structural elements of TAPBPR that lie outside the scoop loop.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The remodeling of MHC I by TAPBPR appears to be induced primarily by structural elements of TAPBPR that lie outside the scoop loop.
source: This remodeling is made possible by the intrinsic plasticity of MHC I molecules (Bailey et al., 2015; Garstka et al., 2011; McShan et al., 2019; Natarajan et al., 2018; Thomas and Tampé, 2017b; van Hateren et al., 2017; van Hateren et al., 2015; Wieczorek et al., 2017), and it appears to be induced primarily by structural elements of TAPBPR that lie outside the scoop loop.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that TAPBPRΔSL can still catalyze peptide displacement.

claim: The TAPBPRΔSL mutant lacking the scoop loop is still able to catalyze peptide displacement because the remodeling is induced primarily by structural elements outside the scoop loop.
source: As a result, the TAPBPRΔSL mutant lacking the scoop loop is still able to catalyze peptide displacement.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from peptide exchange assays.

claim: Once the suboptimal peptide has been released, the scoop loop occupies the position of the peptide C terminus in the F-pocket region.
source: Once the suboptimal peptide has been released, the scoop loop occupies the position of the peptide C terminus in the F-pocket region.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure and experimental data.

claim: The scoop loop contributes to the stabilization of the peptide-deficient binding groove.
source: The scoop loop thereby contributes to the stabilization of the peptide-deficient binding groove.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from SEC analyses.

claim: The scoop loop functions as a peptide selectivity filter by impeding re-binding of the replaced peptide, either through direct competition with the C terminus of the incoming replacement peptide or through an allosteric mechanism.
source: Our two-step peptide exchange — mimicking a peptide-depleted environment — demonstrates that the scoop loop functions at the same time as a peptide selectivity filter by impeding re-binding of the replaced peptide, either through direct competition with the C terminus of the incoming replacement peptide or through an allosteric mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-step peptide exchange assays.

claim: The scoop loop contributes to the significant affinity decrease of incoming peptides for the MHC I groove in the presence of TAPBPR.
source: Hence, the scoop loop contributes to the significant affinity decrease of incoming peptides for the MHC I groove in the presence of TAPBPR (McShan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research and experimental data from the current study.

claim: Assuming a mode of direct competition, the replacement peptide would dock in the MHC I groove first with its N terminus, before it competes with the TAPBPR scoop loop over the F pocket region.
source: Assuming a mode of direct competition, the replacement peptide would dock in the MHC I groove first with its N terminus, before it competes with the TAPBPR scoop loop over the F pocket region (Hafstrand et al., 2019; Thomas and Tampé, 2017a).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on structural considerations and citations.

claim: Negative allosteric coupling between different parts of the MHC I molecule might play a role in the final release of TAPBPR.
source: Negative allosteric coupling between different parts of the MHC I molecule might play a role in the final release of TAPBPR (McShan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on citation to prior research.

claim: The shorter scoop loop in Tsn suggests that its selective pressure on the replacement peptide is weaker than in TAPBPR.
source: The shorter scoop loop in Tsn suggests that its selective pressure on the replacement peptide is weaker than in TAPBPR.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison and experimental data.

claim: Fluorescence polarization and SEC analyses show that the tapasin scoop loop in TAPBPRTsn-SL is less efficient in preventing re-binding of dissociated peptide.
source: Indeed, our fluorescence polarization and SEC analyses show that the tapasin scoop loop in TAPBPRTsn-SL is less efficient in preventing re-binding of dissociated peptide.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-step peptide exchange assays and SEC analyses.

claim: Tsn functions within the PLC, a 'nanocompartment' characterized by an abundant and diverse supply of optimal peptides, reaching a bulk concentration of up to 16 µM before the TAP transporter is arrested by trans-inhibition.
source: Physiologically, these observations might be explained by the fact that Tsn functions within the PLC, a 'nanocompartment' characterized by an abundant and diverse supply of optimal peptides, reaching a bulk concentration of up to 16 µM before the TAP transporter is arrested by trans-inhibition (Grossmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Tsn is supported by other PLC chaperones in stabilizing empty MHC I clients.
source: Moreover, Tsn is supported by other PLC chaperones in stabilizing empty MHC I clients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PLC.

claim: TAPBPR operates as a single MHC I-dedicated chaperone outside the PLC in environments where the concentration of high-affinity peptides is drastically lower.
source: In contrast, TAPBPR operates as a single MHC I-dedicated chaperone outside the PLC in environments where the concentration of high-affinity peptides is drastically lower and MHC I clients have to be stabilized in a peptide-receptive state for extended periods of time.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TAPBPR function.

claim: MHC I clients have to be stabilized in a peptide-receptive state for extended periods of time in the environments where TAPBPR operates.
source: In contrast, TAPBPR operates as a single MHC I-dedicated chaperone outside the PLC in environments where the concentration of high-affinity peptides is drastically lower and MHC I clients have to be stabilized in a peptide-receptive state for extended periods of time.
evidence: This is inferred from the function and localization of TAPBPR.

claim: Long-term stabilization of suboptimally-loaded or empty MHC I by TAPBPR allows the major ER/cis-Golgi glycoprotein folding sensor UGGT1 to re-glucosylate the MHC I molecule.
source: Long-term stabilization of suboptimally-loaded or empty MHC I by TAPBPR also allows the major ER/cis-Golgi glycoprotein folding sensor UGGT1 (UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1) to re-glucosylate the MHC I molecule in order to feed it back into the calnexin/calreticulin cycle and/or allow recruitment of the MHC I to the PLC (Neerincx et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Re-glucosylation of MHC I by UGGT1 feeds it back into the calnexin/calreticulin cycle and/or allows recruitment of the MHC I to the PLC.
source: Long-term stabilization of suboptimally-loaded or empty MHC I by TAPBPR also allows the major ER/cis-Golgi glycoprotein folding sensor UGGT1 (UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1) to re-glucosylate the MHC I molecule in order to feed it back into the calnexin/calreticulin cycle and/or allow recruitment of the MHC I to the PLC (Neerincx et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The scoop loop is evolutionarily fine-tuned to enable Tsn and TAPBPR to accomplish their dual function as chaperone and proofreader in the specific subcellular location they operate in.
source: In conclusion, the evidence provided by our study indicates that the scoop loop is evolutionarily fine-tuned to enable Tsn and TAPBPR to accomplish their dual function as chaperone and proofreader in the specific subcellular location they operate in.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing differential scoop loop functions.

claim: By serving both as a stabilizing element and as selectivity filter in TAPBPR, the scoop loop influences peptide editing.
source: By serving both as a stabilizing element and as selectivity filter in TAPBPR, the scoop loop influences peptide editing and impacts the repertoire of MHC I-associated epitopes presented on the cell surface.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The scoop loop impacts the repertoire of MHC I-associated epitopes presented on the cell surface.
source: By serving both as a stabilizing element and as selectivity filter in TAPBPR, the scoop loop influences peptide editing and impacts the repertoire of MHC I-associated epitopes presented on the cell surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing the scoop loop's role in peptide selection.

claim: HLA-A*02:01 is the major MHC I allomorph in the Caucasian population and found in more than 50% of the global population.
source: HLA-A*02:01, the major MHC I allomorph in the Caucasian population and found in more than 50% of the global population, presents a diverse spectrum of immunodominant autoimmune, viral, and tumor epitopes and is therefore medically highly relevant (Boucherma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: During peptide exchange, MHC I molecules go through a peptide-free high-energy intermediate state after peptide release and before re-entry of a new peptide.
source: During peptide exchange, MHC I molecules go through a peptide-free high-energy intermediate state after peptide release and before re-entry of a new peptide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC I peptide exchange.

claim: A hallmark of peptide editors like TAPBPR is their ability to recognize and chaperone the peptide-free intermediate until it is located in a peptide-rich environment where a high-affinity peptide ligand can enter the MHC I binding groove.
source: A hallmark of peptide editors like TAPBPR is their ability to recognize and chaperone this intermediate until it is located in a peptide-rich environment where a high-affinity peptide ligand can enter the MHC I binding groove (Thomas and Tampé, 2019; Thomas and Tampé, 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The residue in TAPBPR (E105) corresponding to the mutated residue in Tsn-TN3 forms a hydrogen bond with the swung-out Y84 of the MHC heavy chain.
source: According to the TAPBPR-MHC I crystal structures (Jiang et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2017a), the residue in TAPBPR (E105) corresponding to the mutated residue in Tsn-TN3 forms a hydrogen bond with the swung-out Y84 of the MHC heavy chain, which is involved in coordinating the C-terminus of the peptide in liganded MHC.
evidence: This is based on crystal structures cited in the manuscript.

claim: Y84 of the MHC heavy chain is involved in coordinating the C-terminus of the peptide in liganded MHC.
source: According to the TAPBPR-MHC I crystal structures (Jiang et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2017a), the residue in TAPBPR (E105) corresponding to the mutated residue in Tsn-TN3 forms a hydrogen bond with the swung-out Y84 of the MHC heavy chain, which is involved in coordinating the C-terminus of the peptide in liganded MHC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC I structure.

source: Two of the mutated residues in TN6 (R210 and Q212) are part of the jack hairpin of TAPBPR and form several interactions with MHC I heavy-chain residues, while Q275 lies in the interface with the α2–1 helix and the β8 sheet in the floor of the MHC I binding groove.
